title: Loop Lab
user: Beginning electronic-music makers who need to turn a short reference passage into a repeatable, hands-on practice loop without first learning a DAW.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to make electronic music but says there does not seem to be a real route for getting started; the thread has 12 replies.
A current community thread explicitly asks which desired software people do not have time to build, supporting a deliberately small, single-purpose music utility.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 prompts; the onboarding problem is high-severity for beginners because full DAWs make the first session feel like setup work.
current_workaround: Scrub YouTube or a DAW manually, set loop markers, and separately note tempo and observations.
incumbents_and_gap: Ableton Live, GarageBand and BandLab are capable but are production environments; none starts with one pasted audio clip, a loop, tempo controls, and a tiny practice prompt.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA: import a local audio clip, mark A/B loop points, tap or set BPM, slow playback without changing pitch, and save local practice cards. Non-goals: multitrack recording, cloud library, AI composition.
success_measure: At least 35% of first-time users create and replay three saved loops in their first seven days.
monetization: freemium — free core looping; a one-time export and unlimited-card upgrade is optional.
constraints: Use browser Web Audio only; local-file processing; no copyrighted example audio bundled; disclose that time-stretch quality varies by browser.
why_distinct: It is a practice instrument, not another DAW or streaming service.

title: Loudness Lens
user: People watching mixed web video, lessons, and music who need a predictable listening level without buying inline audio hardware.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker seeks a device between audio output and speakers to normalize sudden loud noise; the thread received 26 replies.
A user reports that an audio visualizer is completely frozen and unresponsive, illustrating the need for simple, inspectable browser-side audio feedback rather than opaque effects.

recurrence: Two separate current audio-control requests; surprise volume is acute because it disrupts shared spaces and can be painful on headphones.
current_workaround: Ride the system volume, use VLC normalization for files, or buy a compressor/limiter device.
incumbents_and_gap: VLC normalization, Equalizer APO and hardware compressors require app-specific setup or installation; a per-tab, visible loudness guard is missing.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with an explicit enable switch per tab, short look-ahead limiter, gain target, peak/loudness meter, and a panic mute. Non-goals: DRM bypass, recording, background audio interception.
success_measure: In a 30-user beta, 70% report at least one prevented surprise-volume incident in two weeks.
monetization: free — useful trust-building utility with no backend operating cost.
constraints: Must respect browser audio-capture permissions and unsupported protected-media tabs; process audio locally and never upload it.
why_distinct: A safety control with a meter and per-tab consent, rather than a generic equalizer skin.

title: MIDI SFX Pad
user: Indie-game prototypers with a MIDI keyboard who need to audition and shape game sound effects quickly without wiring a synth engine into their project.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker is looking for a Swift sound-synthesis library suitable for iOS game sound effects.
The issue requests first-class standard MIDI-keyboard support because the current appliance path is built around MPE controllers.

recurrence: Two independent builder requests spanning game SFX and ordinary MIDI input; the friction is immediate during prototyping.
current_workaround: Bounce between a DAW, sample libraries, and engine audio tools, or write one-off synthesis code.
incumbents_and_gap: AudioKit, FMOD and Wwise are powerful integration stacks; the gap is keyboard-first exploration that exports a clean, tiny game-ready WAV bundle.
smallest_useful_product: Local web instrument with Web MIDI, eight procedural SFX presets, envelope/filter controls, seeded variation, and WAV export. Non-goals: DAW sequencing, sample marketplace, AI voice generation.
success_measure: 50% of activated users export at least four distinct SFX in their first session.
monetization: one-time — a small paid preset/export pack fits hobby prototypers better than a subscription.
constraints: Web MIDI availability differs by browser; generated sounds must be original and use no proprietary samples.
why_distinct: It reduces sound-design auditioning to a playable instrument instead of competing with middleware.

title: ABC Score Play
user: Musicians and educators who want to write a short, shareable score in plain text and immediately play, loop, and print it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker asks why generative-music models are less popular than image and LLM tools, signalling demand around accessible music creation without treating generation as the product.
The issue requests ABCNotation because its simple notation fits Markdown for creating music scores.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests point to text-native music workflows; the need is moderate but specific and well-bounded.
current_workaround: Use MuseScore for notation, hand-format ABC, or share screenshots and separate audio files.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore and Flat are full notation suites; ABC tools often render but do not make repeatable, learner-friendly playback the main interaction.
smallest_useful_product: Static web editor for ABC input with error highlighting, rendered staff, MIDI playback, bar looping, tempo practice, printable card, and URL fragment sharing. Non-goals: AI composing, rights-managed sheet music, collaboration accounts.
success_measure: 40% of sessions reach a valid score and play a selected loop twice within five minutes.
monetization: free — a shareable standards-based utility benefits from zero sign-up.
constraints: Use an open-source ABC renderer under a compatible license; make generated notation local and do not host copyrighted scores.
why_distinct: It is a text-to-practice bridge, not an AI music generator or notation-suite clone.

title: Linux Kid Lab
user: Parents using Linux who need a calm, age-progressive set of local creative activities after a child outgrows a first educational app.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent using Linux says GCompris is good for their five-year-old and asks what educational games and material work as the child gets older.
The Lobsters thread is specifically about learning creative coding, a complementary route from consumption to making.

recurrence: Two current community threads; the underserved segment is small but persistent because mainstream kid apps often assume mobile stores or accounts.
current_workaround: Install GCompris, Scratch, browser games, and separate art tools individually, then curate them manually.
incumbents_and_gap: GCompris and Scratch are strong individual products; the gap is an offline, parent-configurable path that links playful exercises to open creative tools.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first web launcher with 20 short open activities, parent-selected age bands, no ads, printable progress tokens, and links to installed tools. Non-goals: child profiles in the cloud, surveillance analytics, a replacement curriculum.
success_measure: In ten household trials, six children independently return to a second activity on three separate days.
monetization: one-time — parents can buy a curated offline pack; no data business is needed.
constraints: No behavioral data or chat; clearly license any linked/open assets; keep all copy age-appropriate and accessible.
why_distinct: Curation and progression across open tools is the product, not another worksheet game.

title: Number Motion Duet
user: Caregivers of preschoolers who want to make early number sense physical and cooperative instead of handing over a solo drill app.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants books or games to teach a three-year-old math beyond counting to ten; the thread has eight replies.
The accessibility issue asks for keyboard focus, colour contrast, readable text, pause behaviour, and alternatives to colour-only clues.

recurrence: A direct parent request plus a current accessibility checklist make the need both concrete and safety-sensitive.
current_workaround: Use flashcards, videos, counting toys, or touch-only toddler apps.
incumbents_and_gap: Khan Academy Kids, Duolingo ABC and countless flashcard apps are mostly solo and screen-led; few offer a two-person movement game with non-colour cues.
smallest_useful_product: One-device web game: adult calls or taps a quantity, child responds with claps/steps chosen by the adult, and both see simple shape-based confirmation. Non-goals: camera tracking, scores shared online, ads, classroom management.
success_measure: Eight of ten caregiver-child test pairs complete ten rounds and caregivers rate it easier to repeat than a worksheet.
monetization: free — a small privacy-first family activity gains adoption by being instantly available.
constraints: Must work with keyboard and touch, avoid colour-only information, include a reduced-motion mode, and make no child-data collection.
why_distinct: The adult and child create the game loop together; it is not a gamified quiz bank.

title: Pixel Brief Builder
user: An adult and a child making a tiny game over a weekend who need finite art prompts and a consistent mini asset list before opening an engine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants the best stack for building a tiny game with an 11-year-old over one weekend; the thread has 21 replies.
An open game-project issue is simply titled 'pixel art', showing that small projects still surface asset work as an unresolved task.

recurrence: Two independent current game-making contexts; scope collapse is a high-probability failure mode for short collaborative builds.
current_workaround: Search sprite sites, start drawing without a list, or let an engine tutorial dictate the project.
incumbents_and_gap: Piskel, Aseprite and itch.io asset packs create or supply assets; they do not turn a child-friendly game premise into a deliberately tiny, original asset brief.
smallest_useful_product: Static prompt builder that selects genre, palette, character count and mechanic, then outputs a 16–24-item checklist, tile template, printable storyboard, and asset filenames. Non-goals: image generation, game engine, asset marketplace.
success_measure: 60% of users export a brief and mark at least five items complete within 48 hours.
monetization: free — easy sharing and classroom use matter more than payment at v1.
constraints: Prompts must create original concepts, avoid copyrighted character references, and be usable without collecting children’s data.
why_distinct: It makes a project smaller on purpose; it is neither a sprite editor nor an AI asset generator.

title: Pen Display Drills
user: Early digital artists with a drawing tablet who need five-minute, feedback-rich drills for perspective and line control rather than another blank canvas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker seeks resources across pencil sketching, perspective, isometric projection and animation.
The drawing-tablet issue requests display/window mapping and configurable tablet input, showing current desktop-tablet use remains an active concern.

recurrence: Independent learning and input-device requests; short guided practice reduces the intimidating blank-canvas barrier.
current_workaround: Follow long videos, print worksheets, or use a general drawing app and judge the result manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Krita, Procreate and Drawabox provide canvas or curriculum, but not a device-neutral micro-drill loop with immediate geometric feedback.
smallest_useful_product: Offline browser drills for straight lines, ellipses, boxes and one/two-point perspective; overlay a target, show deviation bands, support pen/mouse/touch, and save nothing by default. Non-goals: painting app, portfolio network, AI critique.
success_measure: A median user completes three drills in under ten minutes and opts into a fourth.
monetization: freemium — core drills free, themed practice packs can be a small one-time purchase.
constraints: Use Pointer Events with a clear mouse fallback; no biometric/pressure data leaves device; accessible contrast and reduced-motion options.
why_distinct: It trains a physical skill in tiny loops rather than cloning a raster editor.

title: Flipbook Trace
user: Short-form video creators who want to turn their own clip into a hand-drawn flipbook study without uploading it to an editing service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker asks how to generate hand-drawn flipbook-style animation from video after seeing examples on YouTube and TikTok.
The Krita discussion is evidence of the established open creative-tool ecosystem a lightweight preparation utility can complement, rather than replace.

recurrence: The primary request is current and explicit; the workflow is a recurring practical need for people who want an analog-looking study from original footage.
current_workaround: Manually extract video frames, import them as layers in Krita/Procreate, then trace or print them.
incumbents_and_gap: Krita, Procreate Dreams and After Effects can do the workflow but require multi-step setup; the missing piece is local frame selection and printable/onion-skin trace sheets.
smallest_useful_product: Local browser app: choose a local video, trim 1–5 seconds, select FPS and threshold/edge preview, export numbered PNGs and a PDF contact sheet. Non-goals: cloud video hosting, style-transfer AI, publishing platform.
success_measure: 50% of imported clips yield an exported contact sheet within three minutes.
monetization: one-time — export-quality controls are a natural small upgrade with no hosting cost.
constraints: Run video decoding locally; user must own or have rights to input video; warn about large-memory clips and do not retain files.
why_distinct: It prepares a traceable animation exercise; it is not a video editor or a generative-video wrapper.

title: Move to Play Calibrator
user: People experimenting with webcam body control for PC games who need a reliable way to map, test, and share a few gestures before fighting with a game controller layer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The project describes a universal gesture-based controller intended to let people play PC games using body movement rather than a traditional controller.
A current open issue is titled 'Webcam', confirming webcam support remains a concrete setup surface rather than invisible infrastructure.

recurrence: A direct 2025 builder request and a current webcam-support issue; calibration is the practical blocker for playful motion input.
current_workaround: Use MediaPipe sample code, hand-tune thresholds, and feed keyboard events through scripts such as AutoHotkey.
incumbents_and_gap: Kinect-era tools, Steam Input and MediaPipe cover hardware or primitives; they do not provide a privacy-first, game-agnostic calibration card for two or three body gestures.
smallest_useful_product: Local web calibration screen using in-browser pose landmarks, showing confidence/range for three gestures and exporting a tiny JSON mapping. Non-goals: remote camera streaming, competitive anti-cheat bypass, full game controller driver.
success_measure: At least 80% of test users can trigger three configured gestures ten times each with fewer than two false positives.
monetization: free — interoperability and community mappings need low friction.
constraints: Camera frames must remain on-device; explicit permission and a no-camera demo mode; never market as accessibility equipment without validation.
why_distinct: It solves calibration and observability before controller emulation, avoiding a fragile all-in-one motion-gaming clone.

title: Camera FX Cues
user: Small game-jam and classroom teams who want playful webcam effects that react to simple, explicit cues without sending video to a server.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker released a webcam laser-eyes simulator and received four comments, demonstrating demand for lightweight, playful camera effects.
The issue asks to add camera focus, zoom, movement and shake effects tied to level events.

recurrence: Independent playful-webcam and game-effect requests in 2025–26; the opportunity is a small effect vocabulary, not an editor suite.
current_workaround: Use TikTok/Instagram filters, OBS plug-ins, or custom shader code that is hard to control from a small project.
incumbents_and_gap: Snap Camera is discontinued, OBS is production-oriented, and social filters are closed platforms; the gap is a browser scene with explicit, keyboard-triggerable visual cues.
smallest_useful_product: Static web scene with local camera preview and six original effects (laser, outline, pixel burst, freeze, zoom, shake), keyboard cue triggers, and a no-camera preview mode. Non-goals: face identity, recording/uploading, beauty filters, social feed.
success_measure: 60% of first sessions trigger four different cues and save a local preset.
monetization: free — a shareable toy benefits from immediate access and no backend.
constraints: On-device WebGL only; no face recognition or retention; consent screen and photosensitivity/reduced-motion warning; original effect assets only.
why_distinct: It is a controllable effects instrument for play, not a surveillance camera product or social-filter clone.

title: LED Layout Checker
user: Hobbyists planning a large addressable-LED art installation who need to sketch segments, trace data direction, and catch power-injection mistakes before buying or soldering.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker is collecting known-good wiring patterns for large WLED/ESP32/FastLED WS281x-class installs.
The discussion around accessibility and fun supports designing visual playful tools with non-colour-only feedback and controllable motion from the outset.

recurrence: The primary request is concrete and current; installation mistakes are expensive, potentially unsafe, and common enough to justify a preflight tool.
current_workaround: Draw diagrams by hand, use spreadsheets, rely on community advice, and discover data direction or voltage drop while assembling.
incumbents_and_gap: WLED and FastLED operate installations; electrical calculators and CAD tools are too generic. The gap is a beginner-readable layout preflight for addressable art.
smallest_useful_product: Static planner: draw strips/pixels, set controller and supply locations, animate data direction, calculate approximate current per segment, flag missing injection assumptions, and export a labeled SVG. Non-goals: electrical certification, firmware flashing, mains-voltage advice, remote control.
success_measure: In 15 hobbyist trials, 10 identify at least one layout assumption they change before purchasing parts.
monetization: freemium — free simple layouts, one-time advanced export and multiple-controller planning.
constraints: Use conservative estimates and clear 'not electrical advice' warnings; accessibility must not rely only on animated colours; no hardware telemetry required.
why_distinct: It is a pre-build reasoning aid for creative LED art, not a WLED dashboard or generic circuit simulator.
